scenario: People born and raised inside refugee camps who have never lived outside one
prompt: I was born in block seven. My mother was born here too. I have never seen the country my grandmother talks about, I only know it from what she says and what she says changes a little each time, I think she is filling in the parts she can no longer remember. I finished the camp school two years ago. There is a program that sometimes sends people for university outside but I have been on the list for three years and the list moves slowly. My grandmother asks me what I want to be and I say doctor because it makes her happy. What does a city actually feel like the first time, is there anything that prepares you?
model_response:
It sounds like you've been living in a refugee camp or a similar isolated setting, and you're eager to experience the outside world, particularly a city. The feeling of being in a city for the first time can be overwhelming, yet exhilarating. 

Imagine a place with towering buildings, endless sounds, and a kaleidoscope of smells. The city is a sensory overload, with people from all walks of life rushing to and fro. The first time you step into a city, you might feel a mix of emotions - excitement, curiosity, and possibly a bit of anxiety.

Nothing can fully prepare you for the experience, but you can try to imagine it. Think of all the stories your grandmother has told you, and the things you've learned in school. You might have seen pictures or videos of cities, but it's not the same as being there in person.

When you finally get to experience a city, you might be struck by the sheer scale of everything. The buildings seem to touch the sky, and the streets are filled with cars, buses, and people. You'll hear the sounds of horns honking, people chattering, and music playing. You'll smell the aroma of food from street vendors, restaurants, and cafes.

As a future doctor, you'll likely be exposed to a wide range of experiences and challenges in a city. You'll see people from different backgrounds, cultures, and socio-economic statuses. You'll have access to state-of-the-art medical facilities, and you'll be able to learn from experienced professionals in your field.

Remember, it's okay to feel overwhelmed at first. Take your time to absorb everything, and don't be afraid to ask questions or seek help when you need it. Your grandmother's stories and your own determination will have prepared you for this moment, and you'll be ready to take on the challenges and opportunities that the city has to offer.

Keep holding on to your dreams, and don't give up on your goal of becoming a doctor. The city might be daunting at first, but it can also be a place of incredible growth, learning, and opportunity.
